item.title: Battle of Cervera
item.description: The Battle of Cervera took place near Espinosa de Cervera on 29 July 1000 between the Christian troops of counts Sancho García of Castile and García Gómez of Saldaña and the Muslim Caliphate of Córdoba under the hajib Almanzor. The battle, "tremendous and difficult to describe", was a victory for Almanzor. The battle is listed as the fifty-second of Almanzor's career in the Dikr bilad al-Andalus.

item.title: Battle of Trafalgar
item.description: The Battle of Trafalgar was a fleet action fought on 21 October 1805 off Cape Trafalgar between the Royal Navy and a combined fleet of the French and Spanish navies during the Trafalgar campaign of the War of the Third Coalition. As part of Napoleon's planned invasion of the United Kingdom, the French and Spanish navies planned to take control of the English Channel and provide the French invasion army with safe passage to England. A Franco-Spanish fleet under French Vice-admiral Pierre-Charles Villeneuve sailed from Cádiz on 18 October 1805 and three days later encountered a British fleet under Vice-Admiral of the White Horatio Nelson, 1st Viscount Nelson in the Atlantic along southwestern Spain. Nelson sailed his fleet directly at the Franco-Spanish line of battle's flank in two columns, hoping to break the line into pieces. Villeneuve foresaw Nelson's tactic but failed to prepare for it; the crews of the French and Spanish ships in contrast to their British counterparts were inexperienced, poorly trained and suffered from low morale. Nelson's plan worked brilliantly with both columns splitting the Franco-Spanish fleet in three groups, isolating the rear. The Franco-Spanish vanguard sailed ahead while attempting to turn back, leaving the British temporarily superior in number against the remainder of Villeneuve's fleet. 18 French and Spanish ships were ultimately captured or destroyed while the British lost none. Nelson's approach exposed the leading ships of the British columns to intense crossfire as they approached the Franco-Spanish lines. Nelson's own HMS Victory led the front column and was almost knocked out of action. Nelson was shot by French marksman during the battle and died shortly before it ended. Villeneuve was captured along with his flagship and later attended Nelson's state funeral while a captive on parole in Britain. Following the battle, the senior surviving Spanish commander, Lieutenant-general Federico Gravina, led part of the surviving Franco-Spanish fleet away from the storm; he died six months later of wounds sustained during the battle. Nelson's victory against the odds and death during battle secured his place as a British national hero. His signal to the fleet shortly before the battle, "England expects that every man will do his duty", is regularly quoted and paraphrased. The victory confirmed Britain's naval supremacy in the Napoleonic Wars and was achieved in part through Nelson's departure from prevailing sailing ship tactics. The battle led to the definitive end of any real efforts by Napoleon to invade Britain, and although it had a limited impact on the War of the Third Coalition resulted in Britain's command of the sea not being tested for over a century.
